**WSA formula (Eq. 1 in the paper):**

$$v_{r}(f_{s},\theta_{b})=v_{slow}+\frac{v_{fast}-v_{slow}}{(1+f_{s})^{\alpha}}\left[\beta-\gamma e^{-(\theta_{b}/\omega)^{\delta}}\right]^{\iota}$$

**Attribution:** "is the Wang-Sheeley-Arge (WSA) model" is cited to Arge et al. 2003. The paper gives no 2004 attribution.

- **Title:** "Improved method for specifying solar wind speed near the sun"
- **Authors:** C. N. Arge, D. Odstrčil, V. J. Pizzo, and L. R. Mayer
- **Journal:** AIP Conference Proceedings, 679(1), 190–193 (2003)

**Coefficients:** The paper does not report values for the WSA coefficients (α, β, γ, δ, ι, ω, v_slow, v_fast). It says only that "There are eight free parameters, including the fast and slow wind speed." The only values given are for the authors' modified formula (Eq. 4), not WSA: v_slow = 200 km/s, v_fast = 700 km/s, ω = 7, and δ = 1/2.5, as a "first rough parameter fit."

Links: [{"title":"A variational approach to Data Assimilation in the Solar Wind","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07306"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.06362v3"},{"title":"close this message","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.06362v2"},{"title":"reading-clone.eprints-hosting.org","url":"https://reading-clone.eprints-hosting.org/79992"},{"title":"Improving solar wind forecasting using Data Assimilation","url":"https://deepai.org/publication/improving-solar-wind-forecasting-using-data-assimilation"},{"title":"Matthew Lang","url":"https://ras.ac.uk/poster-contest/matthew-lang"},{"title":"EGU21 2771 presentation","url":"https://presentations.copernicus.org/EGU21/EGU21-2771_presentation.pdf"},{"title":"met spate","url":"https://research.reading.ac.uk/met-spate/?p=498"},{"title":"Lang et al 2018 Space Weather","url":"https://reading-9.eprints-hosting.org/79992/1/Lang_et_al-2018-Space_Weather.pdf"}]

The Lang and Owens paper is in *Space Weather* (2019, vol. 17, pp. 59–83, DOI 10.1029/2018SW001857). It is the first variational data assimilation scheme for the solar wind, built on a simple solar-wind propagation model.

- **Headline result:** Using STEREO data, the assimilation improved the near-Earth solar wind estimate for 12 of 13 Carrington Rotations. The reported root-mean-square error reduction is 18.4% with a 18.4% reduction in the root-mean-squared-error.
- **Where the gains came from:** The largest improvements occurred when the steady-state assumption of coronal models failed (during times when the steady-state assumption of the coronal models breaks down).
- **Scope:** The study covers Oct 2010 to Oct 2011, when STEREO was roughly 80° from Earth. It also tested synthetic observations.
- **Caveat from the authors:** They note the pure variational approach is technically hard to apply to complex solar-wind models, and suggest hybrid methods as a simpler alternative.
- **Later follow-up:** A 2020/2021 preprint by Lang and collaborators (arXiv:2012.06362) extends this to 2007–2014 with the HUXt model and reports a 31.4% reduction in solar wind speed root mean-square error (RMSE) for DA-initialised forecasts versus non-DA forecasts. The search results did not clearly tie this figure to the 2019 paper, so keep the two separate.

I did not find the term "BRaVDA" in these results, so I could not confirm how the 2019 paper relates to it.

Links: [{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.06362v3"},{"title":"close this message","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.06362v2"},{"title":"EGU21 2771 presentation","url":"https://presentations.copernicus.org/EGU21/EGU21-2771_presentation.pdf"},{"title":"reading-clone.eprints-hosting.org","url":"https://reading-clone.eprints-hosting.org/98785/9/2020SW002698.pdf"},{"title":"EGU21 2771","url":"https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU21/EGU21-2771.html"},{"title":"We gratefully acknowledge support from","url":"https://export.arxiv.org/abs/2012.06362"},{"title":"loading page","url":"https://essopenarchive.org/users/555501/articles/628410-solar-wind-data-assimilation-in-an-operational-context-use-of-near-real-time-data-and-the-forecast-value-of-an-l5-monitor"},{"title":"Space Weather (May 2023)","url":"https://doaj.org/article/a35dac9c12874214bf69c3a87d44b597"},{"title":"reading-clone.eprints-hosting.org","url":"https://reading-clone.eprints-hosting.org/79992"}]

The paper exists and matches your citation details. It is Lang, Witherington, Turner, Owens and Riley, published in Space Weather in 2021 (volume 19, issue 7) under DOI 10.1029/2020SW002698. The authors describe it as an open-access article under a CC-BY license.

On the RMSE figure, the sources differ in detail. An early submitted manuscript's key points report a 31.4% reduction in solar wind speed root mean-square error (RMSE) compared to forecasts with no DA. The published version's summary describes the gain as roughly a third: it says that on average over the 7-year period, DA can reduce forecast errors by around a third, using 27-day forecasts over STEREO-B's operational lifetime. I did not find the published article's exact RMSE percentage in these results, so the 31.4% figure likely comes from the pre-publication manuscript and should be checked against the final paper before citing.

The study also addresses STEREO-B's latitude offset. The manuscript's key points note that DA can remove significant positive correlations between forecast RMSE and latitude of STEREO-B, and the published summary says DA is able to reduce biases from available spacecraft observations being misaligned with Earth.

The method uses a variational DA scheme with the HUXt solar wind model and observations from STEREO-A, STEREO-B and ACE. The scheme lets solar-wind observations far from the Sun, such as at 1 AU, update the inner boundary conditions of the solar wind model at 30 solar radii.

- **Model:** HUXt, described as a "computationally efficient solar wind model." It is not MAS. The 30 solar radii inner boundary is the only related detail.
- **Period:** 27-day forecasts over STEREO-B's operational lifetime, 01 November 2007 to 30 September 2014.
- **RMSE:** "We find that 27-day root mean-square error (RMSE) for STEREO-B corotation and DA forecasts are comparable." Both are described as significantly lower than non-DA forecasts. No numerical RMSE reduction is given.

The paper is Turner et al. (2023), published in *Space Weather* vol. 21, no. 5, DOI 10.1029/2023SW003457. The authors are Harriet Turner, Matthew Lang, Mathew Owens, Andy Smith, Pete Riley, Mike Marsh, and Siegfried Gonzi.

- **Purpose:** The study addresses the gap that earlier assimilation experiments used science-quality data, not the near-real-time feeds an operational system would receive. Those earlier experiments were the first to show that assimilating in situ solar wind speed could improve forecasts near Earth. (Initial experiments with assimilation of in situ solar wind speed observations suggest the potential for significant improvement in the forecast skill of near‐Earth solar wind conditions. However, these experiments have assimilated science‐quality observations, rather than near‐real‐time (NRT) data)
- **Data:** The team assimilated both NRT and science data from STEREO, plus near-Earth observations from ACE and DSCOVR. (Here, we assimilate both NRT and science observations from the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) and near‐Earth observations from the Advanced Composition Explorer and Deep Space Climate Observatory spacecraft.)
- **Key result:** NRT-based forecasts performed about as well as science-data forecasts, which the authors read as support for an operational scheme. (An operational solar wind DA scheme would provide significant forecast improvement, with reduction in the mean absolute error of solar wind speed around 46% over forecasts without DA.) Note that the ESS Open Archive preprint and the author's seminar abstract give the figure as about 45%, so the published 46% is the one to cite.
- **L5 monitor:** The authors quantified the forecast gain from a proposed L5 monitor, using STEREO and L1 spacecraft configurations as stand-ins. The seminar abstract reports a 15.5% improvement for forecast lead times of less than 5 days when observations from L5 are assimilated alongside those from L1, compared with L1 alone. I did not confirm this figure against the full published text.

Links: [{"title":"LOFAR Newsletter February 2026 - ASTRON Science","url":"https://science.astron.nl/lofar-newsletter-february-2026/"},{"title":"LOFAR Newsletter June 2026 - ASTRON Science","url":"https://science.astron.nl/lofar-newsletter-june-2026/"},{"title":"A decade of sub-arcsecond imaging with the International LOFAR Telescope","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.06946"},{"title":"Real-time station monitor and stationtest pipelines for LOFAR 2.0","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2503.02425v1"},{"title":"Investigating ionospheric calibration for LOFAR 2.0 with simulated observations","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04636"},{"title":"LOFAR Newsletter October 2025 - ASTRON Science","url":"https://science.astron.nl/lofar-newsletter-october-2025/"},{"title":"Cosmic ray detection with the LOFAR radio telescope","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.07681"},{"title":"LOFAR Newsletter March 2025 - ASTRON Science","url":"https://science.astron.nl/lofar-newsletter-march-2025/"},{"title":"Catalogue of Solar Radio Bursts Detected by the LOFAR LV614 Station at the Irbene Observatory during Solar Cycle 25","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.26535"},{"title":"The Dawes Review 13: A New Look at The Dynamic Radio Sky","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.10785"}]

The search didn't turn up anything specific to LOFAR's interplanetary scintillation (IPS) observations or to space weather programs being stopped. The results do describe the overall downtime and upgrade timeline.

- **Start of downtime:** LOFAR1.0 production observations ended with the close of Cycle 20 on 31 August 2024, and the team then moved to completing the LOFAR2.0 upgrade (LOFAR1.0 production observations ended at the end of observing Cycle 20 on 31 August, 2024. Efforts are now being invested into completing the LOFAR2.0 telescope upgrade to start LOFAR2.0 production operations.).
- **Dutch stations:** By October 2025, LOFAR2.0 hardware has been installed in all stations. The February 2026 newsletter says most stations have now been successfully upgraded.
- **International stations:** Their upgrade was still ahead as of early 2026. The February 2026 newsletter says it is scheduled to begin in the second quarter of this year. The June 2026 newsletter reports that the upgrade of station SE607 in Sweden had started in week 17.
- **Commissioning:** The June 2026 newsletter reports that new software- or operating system deployments typically only lead to downtime on the day of the upgrade and sometimes the day after.
- **Related observations:** A solar radio burst study using the Latvian station LV614 says that after September 2024, International LOFAR Telescope observations were discontinued due to the LOFAR 2.0 upgrade, and only single-station observations were conducted.

Still unverified: whether IPS observations specifically stopped, and when they might resume. A follow-up search on LOFAR IPS or space weather observations, or on the LOFAR2.0 Cycle 1 or Open Time start date, would be needed to answer that.

Links: [{"title":"National Aeronautics and Space Administration - PUNCH Level-3 WFI-2 Unpolarized F-Corona Model","url":"https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/punch-level-3-wfi-2-unpolarized-f-corona-model"},{"title":"National Aeronautics and Space Administration - PUNCH Level-3 Polarized Mosaic Starfield Model","url":"https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/punch-level-3-polarized-mosaic-starfield-model"},{"title":"Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH)","url":"https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11207-026-02608-2"},{"title":"National Aeronautics and Space Administration - PUNCH Level-3 WFI-1 Polarized F-Corona Model","url":"https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/punch-level-3-wfi-1-polarized-f-corona-model"},{"title":"Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH)","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.15131"},{"title":"National Aeronautics and Space Administration - PUNCH Level-3 Clear Mosaic Starfield Model","url":"https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/punch-level-3-clear-mosaic-starfield-model"},{"title":"National Aeronautics and Space Administration - PUNCH Level-3 WFI-3 Polarized F-Corona Model","url":"https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/punch-level-3-wfi-3-polarized-f-corona-model"},{"title":"Data Finder - SDAC NASA/GSFC - Solar Data Analysis Center","url":"https://umbra.nascom.nasa.gov/newsite/data.html"},{"title":"PUNCH: News - Southwest Research Institute","url":"https://punch.space.swri.edu/punch_news_archive.php?pagenum=0"}]

The search turned up PUNCH's data archive and policies, but no single announcement of a 2025 Level 3 public data release date.

- **Open access:** PUNCH has an open data policy: all scientific data are released to everyone simultaneously, with no restrictions on use.
- **Where to get it:** PUNCH data are archived and distributed via NASA's Solar Data Analysis Center (SDAC), and may be retrieved directly from the SDAC file system or via the Virtual Solar Observatory (VSO). The SDAC Data Finder lists PUNCH, and PUNCH was launched on 11th March 2025.
- **What Level 3 contains:** Level 3 is the science-ready tier. Level 3 data are background-subtracted and ready for scientific analysis of the K corona and solar wind. Latency is typically 14 days from receipt of the data by the SOC, because background subtraction needs long baselines.
- **Naming:** Data products are identified by their level number, a three-character code, and a timestamp. Image products are named with a leading "P" (Polarized) or "C" (Clear).
- **Current Level 3 datasets on data.gov (SDAC-published):** these include a WFI-2 unpolarized F-corona model with Dataset Last Updated: September 22, 2026, a polarized mosaic starfield model last updated August 31, 2026, and several WFI-1 and WFI-3 polarized F-corona models. Each has a download link to the SDAC mirror at umbra.nascom.nasa.gov/punch/3/.
- **Citation:** Per the PUNCH team, reference to the entire Collection, including the DOI below, should be used when this and other member datasets in the Collection are cited: Southwest Research Institute (2025). PUNCH NFI-WFI Level-3 Science images [Collection]. Solar Data Analysis Center. https://doi.org/10.48322/nnv7-bn21.
- **Acknowledgement:** Users are asked to acknowledge the PUNCH mission with the statement "PUNCH is a heliophysics mission to study the corona, solar wind, and space weather as an integrated system, and is part of NASA's Explorers program (Contract 80GSFC14C0014)".
- **Documentation:** Current information and links to relevant analysis software, documentation, and team contact information may be found at the PUNCH mission website "https://punch.space.swri.edu".

Gap: I did not confirm the exact date Level 3 public release began in 2025. The SDAC and mission site pages would be the place to check that.

Per the search results, CCOR-1 was declared operational in spring 2025, and SWPC publishes its imagery.

- **Operational date conflicts across sources.** SWPC's coronagraph page says CCOR-1 became operational on April 4, 2025. A SolarNews post says the public archive starts February 24, 2025, when CCOR-1 was declared operational. The NRL site instead gives the GOES-19 date: the satellite became officially operational as GOES EAST on April 7, 2025.
- **Pre-operational period.** Before the declaration, SWPC labeled the imagery "preliminary and non-operational."
- **Imagery availability.** SWPC's coronagraph page carries CCOR-1 imagery, with images and data updated every 15 minutes. Archived images are on NCEI, and the data are available at services.swpc.noaa.gov.
- **Switchover.** A SWPC notice says GOES-19 is now fully operational as the new GOES East (replacing GOES-16) and the primary space weather instrument, while GOES-18 continues as GOES West and remains the backup space weather platform.
- **CCOR-2 (lower confidence).** NRL said CCOR-2 was installed on the SWFO-L1 spacecraft, scheduled for launch in Late 2025. A Wikipedia entry instead says CCOR-2 started operating in June 2026. I didn't verify the Wikipedia claim, so treat it as unconfirmed.

Bottom line: the most authoritative sources point to an April 2025 operational declaration (April 4 for CCOR-1, April 7 for GOES-19 as GOES East), with the February 24–25, 2025 dates tied to the start of public preliminary data. I did not find a single primary SWPC declaration notice confirming the exact date.
